source.title: Interpretability as Compression: Reconsidering SAE Explanations of Neural Activations with MDL-SAEs
source.authors: K. Ayonrinde; Michael T. Pearce; Lee Sharkey

page_placements.theme: Sparsity, width and extraction choices determine feature granularity

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses SAEs, sparse features, and superposition, but its MNIST and theoretical results do not test the listed claims about superposition geometry, neuron polysemanticity, or LLM features.
record.gate_note: The paper reports an MNIST SAE case study and theoretical examples about feature splitting and hierarchical coding. These do not measure whether sparse features overlap as nearly orthogonal directions, whether neurons share features because of limited capacity, or whether SAE features are canonical units. The two adjacent findings recorded below are not tests of a listed version.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes an MDL framework for choosing SAE hyperparameters. Its only experiment trains SAEs on raw MNIST pixels, not on a network's activations. Its feature-splitting and hierarchy sections are analytic toy calculations. None of these results measures superposition geometry, capacity-driven polysemanticity, other causes of polysemanticity, LLM feature spread, or 1-D versus multi-dimensional features. The MNIST finding that features change with width and L0 at equal MSE touches on whether SAE features are canonical (V5). It does not bear on V5 itself, because the SAE decomposes the data rather than a model's representation, and the authors draw no conclusion about canonicality.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors argue that description length, not raw sparsity, should guide SAE selection, since it can avoid undesirable feature splitting and favour hierarchical coding. On MNIST the MDL-optimal SAE has stroke-like features. They also note that MDL is used only for model selection over a sweep, not as a training objective.
record.recipe_differences: Does not reproduce or apply the original superposition method; instead it uses an MDL-based SAE model-selection case study on MNIST and theoretical coding examples.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported SAE feature appearances and description lengths vary across high-L0/narrow, low-L0/wide, and MDL-selected settings. The feature-splitting example's preferred representation varies with the correlation between A and B.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained on MNIST pixels at the same test MSE (0.0150) give different features depending on regime. Narrow, high-L0 SAEs give point-like or PCA-like features. Wide, low-L0 SAEs give digit-like exemplars. The MDL-selected SAE gives reusable strokes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At a fixed reconstruction error, the SAE dictionary obtained on MNIST data depends on the width/L0 choice, and MDL selects intermediate stroke-like features.

fits_no_version.finding: In an analytic Boolean toy, splitting off an A∧B feature always lowers L0. Description length favours the split only when A and B are highly correlated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparsity-driven SAE objectives can favour feature splitting that description length would reject, depending on feature co-occurrence.

record.problems: The empirical case study is on MNIST rather than an LLM or a network designed to test superposition. Feature appearance is described qualitatively; the text gives no uncertainty estimates for these comparisons. The paper notes that the point where dead features rise was not tested systematically and may depend on the dataset.
record.rows_left_out: No additional directly claim-relevant results identified. The paper's hierarchical coding discussion is conceptual and does not test any listed version.

untested.parts: No toy superposition model; no measure of feature overlap, orthogonality, sparsity transition or geometry.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity-allocation measurement.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
No LLM SAE trained or evaluated. The GPT-2 bit count is arithmetic from Bloom's published SAE hyperparameters, not a measurement of feature recovery.
No test of completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, or canonicality of SAE features on model activations. The MNIST width/L0 dependence concerns pixel data, not model units.
Directed-tree and subspace decoders are discussed only conceptually. There is no measurement of multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The rows' versions ['none'] and state cannot_determine are appropriate. r3 is the MDL-selected configuration, i.e. the study's own method's selection outcome. Sections 6–7 (feature splitting, hierarchy) are analytic, not empirical. The GPT-2 description-length comparison in Section 4 is computed from published hyperparameters (L0=65, D=25,000) and is not a test of V4. The dead-feature versus DL-rise observation in the appendix was explicitly not tested systematically. Preprint.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test superposition geometry, overlap, feature sparsity transitions, or regular geometry in small networks.
Does not test whether neurons are polysemantic because features compete for capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
Does not measure feature distribution across LLM neurons or recover LLM features with an SAE.
Does not test completeness, stability, or canonicality of SAE features.
Does not test whether features in superposition are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional features.

rows.subject: BatchTopK SAEs trained on MNIST
rows.operation_detail: Selected the SAE hyperparameters with minimum description length among those meeting the reconstruction-error tolerance.
rows.measure: Description length and qualitative feature appearance
rows.value: The selected features appeared as longer digit strokes that could apply to multiple digits; the paper describes this as a meaningful decomposition into reusable and composable features.
rows.note: Adjacent result about SAE feature structure; the study does not test whether these are canonical units or superposed directions.

rows.subject: Toy model of undesirable feature splitting
rows.operation_detail: Compared a representation with two Boolean features to one with three mutually exclusive features, including an explicit A∧B feature.
rows.baseline: No feature splitting: L0 = pA + pB; DL = H(pA) + H(pB).
rows.value: Feature splitting has lower L0, but the paper says it is preferred by description length when correlation is large and avoided when correlation is small.
rows.note: Theoretical toy example about feature splitting and coding costs, not a test of neuron polysemanticity or superposition geometry.

relation.reason: Superposition provides conceptual context; the study neither tests it nor relies on an established superposition result as an experimental tool.

tranche.reason: The MNIST experiment evaluates SAE model selection and qualitative feature structure. The coding arguments address sparsity, splitting and hierarchy without testing any listed superposition claim version.

source_check.notes: Feature appearance is assessed qualitatively on MNIST inputs, not neural-network activations. The authors explicitly use MDL for selection over trained models rather than as a training objective.

statements.correction: Desired test MSE tolerance: 0.0150; MSE variation across hyperparameters: roughly 0.0001. High-L0 narrow SAEs: small digit sections or dense PCA-like features. Low-L0 wide SAEs: full-digit-like features. MDL-selected SAE: longer reusable digit strokes. Section 5; Appendix A.2.
statements.problem: The qualitative comparison is accurate, but 0.0150 is the desired MSE tolerance, not a reported exact test MSE shared by every SAE.
